title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
text:
The problem
Code gets shared. Secrets must not.

An API key typed into a script travels with that script — everywhere.

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
section: Where a hardcoded key ends up
text:
Where a hardcoded key ends up
API_KEY = "sk-abc123yourrealkeyhere"   # never


Git history
Deleting the line later doesn’t help. Old commits keep it.


Shared files
Notebooks, exports, screenshots, screen shares.


Everyone with access
Teammates, forks, and anyone who ever clones the repo.

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
section: The fix: separate config from code
text:
The fix: separate config from code


Your code
no secret inside

←

Environment
API_KEY=…

←

Where it’s stored
.env file · secret store



The code is identical on every machine
Only the environment changes: laptop, server, Databricks
The secret is never committed

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
text:
What is an environment variable?
A named string the operating system hands to your program.
import os

os.getenv("API_KEY")                       # None if missing
os.environ["API_KEY"]                      # KeyError if missing
os.getenv("API_URL", "http://localhost")   # with a default
Always strings. Convert numbers and booleans yourself.

1 · Python
Local development with .env files and the python-dotenv package.


2 · Databricks
Four ways to store an API key, ranked from safest to worst.


Appendix · R
The same idea with .Renviron, askpass, and keyring.

1 Write a .env file

→

2 Ignore it in Git

→

3 Load it in Python


First, install the package:
pip install python-dotenv

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
text:
1 Write a .env file
One NAME=value per line, in your project folder.


.env

API_KEY=sk-abc123yourrealkeyhere
API_URL=https://api.example.com
DEBUG=true


No spaces around =
Quotes only needed if the value has spaces
# starts a comment

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
text:
2 Keep it out of Git


.gitignore

.env

Then commit a template so teammates know what to set:


.env.example

API_KEY=your-key-here
API_URL=https://api.example.com


Add .env to .gitignore before your first commit.

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
text:
3 Load it in Python
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()                      # .env → os.environ

api_key = os.getenv("API_KEY")
api_url = os.getenv("API_URL")
Call load_dotenv() once, at the top of your entry script.

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
text:
Use it, never print it
import requests

resp = requests.get(
    api_url,
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"},
)
print(resp.status_code)


200
Key is valid


401 / 403
Key is wrong or expired

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
section: Fail fast when a key is missing
text:
Fail fast when a key is missing
def require(name):
    value = os.getenv(name)
    if not value:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Missing env var: {name}")
    return value

api_key = require("API_KEY")
A clear error at startup beats a confusing 401 ten minutes later.

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
text:
Handy options
load_dotenv(find_dotenv())      # search parent folders
load_dotenv(".env.dev")         # a specific file
load_dotenv(override=True)      # .env wins over real env

config = dotenv_values(".env")  # a dict, os.environ untouched
By default load_dotenv() does not overwrite variables already set. Servers and CI can override your local file.

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
text:
askpass: type it when needed
# install.packages("askpass")
api_key <- askpass::askpass("Enter your API key")

Pops up a password prompt, typed characters hidden
Returns the value as a string
Nothing is written to disk

Good for quick interactive work. You retype the key each session.

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
text:
keyring: store it once
# install.packages("keyring")
keyring::key_set("my-api")          # prompts once, then stores it
api_key <- keyring::key_get("my-api")

Saved in your OS credential store (Keychain, Credential Manager)
Read it back in any script, no file in your project
Closest R equivalent to Databricks secrets

Never put the key itself in your code. Only the name "my-api".

title: Build a Short Training
text:
You’re teaching, not presenting
A presentation ends when you stop talking. A training ends when they can do it.

Every team owes one. Pick something your project needs, and you’ll learn it properly by teaching it.

title: Build a Short Training
text:
The shape of a training


Frame the need

→

Navigate to details

→

Give examples

→

Let them practice

→

Review / reflect




Slides carry the first two steps.

Code carries the next two.

Frame all of it the way industry would: why a team would pay for this skill.

title: Build a Short Training
text:
1 · Frame the need
One slide. Why should anyone in this room care?

What problem does this solve that we currently solve badly, or not at all?
Where does it show up in our project?
What breaks without it?


If you can’t name the need, don’t teach the tool. Nobody remembers a solution to a problem they never felt.

title: Build a Short Training
text:
2 · Navigate to details
Enough background to follow along, and no more.

The two or three ideas they must hold to read your code
The vocabulary, defined once
Where it sits next to what we already know

Resist teaching the whole API. You are not the documentation.

title: Build a Short Training
text:
3 · Give examples
Working code they can read, on data they recognize.

Start with the smallest version that does something real
Show the output, not just the code
Use our C-Store data where you can, so nobody is learning a new dataset at the same time
Build up in steps: one idea per cell

title: Build a Short Training
text:
4 · Let them practice
This is the part teams skip. It’s the part that works.


Make it runnable
A notebook in our GitHub org, or a Databricks notebook they can clone.


Make it small
Ten minutes, with a clear finish line. Not a project.


Make it graded by them
Give the expected output, so they know whether they got it.


Walk the room while they work. Where they get stuck is your real feedback.

title: Build a Short Training
text:
5 · Review and reflect
Close the loop.

What should they be able to do now that they couldn’t before?
The one mistake you’d bet most of them made
Where to look next: docs, a guide, the book chapter

title: Build a Short Training
text:
What good looks like



DataCamp is the model
Short video, immediate coding, repeat. Never more than a few minutes of talking before you do something.



AI study guides
Fine for building your material and checking your explanation.
Not a substitute for writing the practice activity yourself.

title: Build a Short Training
text:
Your checklist

A need stated in one sentence
Slides for the first two steps, short
Runnable code in our GitHub org, self-contained
A practice activity with an expected output
A takeaway slide and somewhere to go next
A dry run — time it


Copy topics/_training_template.qmd to start. It has these five sections and the course theme already set up.

title: Baskets of Goods
text:
The question
What sells with what?

Every rule you find has to survive one question: what would the store do differently tomorrow?

title: Baskets of Goods
section: A basket is a row per transaction
text:
A basket is a row per transaction


Line items
one row per scan

→

Basket
one row per transaction

→

Rules
one row per rule


A basket is the set of categories in one transaction. Duplicates collapse: two energy drinks count as one Packaged Beverages.

title: Baskets of Goods
text:
Three numbers describe a rule
For a rule A → B:


Support
How often A and B appear together, out of all baskets.
Is it common enough to care?


Confidence
Of baskets with A, how many also have B.
How reliable is the rule?


Lift
Confidence ÷ how often B shows up anyway.
Does A actually tell us anything?


Lift is the one that matters. High confidence on a very common item means nothing.

title: Baskets of Goods
text:
The arithmetic, on our data
Beer → Cigarettes, from the multi-item baskets:




Value
Where it comes from




Support
0.065
6.5% of baskets have both


Confidence
0.318
31.8% of beer baskets also have cigarettes


Cigarettes alone
0.187
18.7% of all baskets have cigarettes


Lift
1.70
0.318 ÷ 0.187



Beer buyers are 1.7× more likely than average to also buy cigarettes.
Example conclusions — one run on the Idaho sample, not a finished analysis.

title: Baskets of Goods
text:
Reading lift


Lift > 1
They go together more than chance. Worth acting on.


Lift ≈ 1
Independent. The rule tells you nothing.


Lift < 1
They repel. Buying A makes B less likely.



Association is not causation. A rule says the two co-occur, not that moving one moves the other. That’s what a test or a promotion proves.

title: Baskets of Goods
text:
What makes C-Store baskets different


Baskets are tiny
A drink. A pack of cigarettes. Fuel only. Support is low for everything.


A few categories dominate
Fuel, tobacco, lottery, and services swamp the counts.


SKUs are too fine
Hundreds of drink SKUs give sparse, unactionable rules. Roll up to category.


Time and place matter
Morning coffee baskets look nothing like Friday-evening beer baskets.

title: Baskets of Goods
text:
Profile first


2.7M line items in the Idaho sample


1.5M baskets, averaging 1.8 items


56% of baskets hold a single item


More than half the data carries no co-occurrence at all. Profile before you mine, or you’ll tune thresholds blind.
Example conclusions — one run on the Idaho sample, not a finished analysis.

title: Baskets of Goods
section: Cleaning: what counts as a basket
text:
Cleaning: what counts as a basket

Single-item baskets: keep them and support collapses; drop them and every number is conditional on “basket had 2+ items.”
Fuel, tobacco, lottery: so common they attach to everything. Tag them, then decide whether they’re items or context.


Every one of these changes your rules. Write the decision down, and report your numbers next to it.

title: Baskets of Goods
text:
Roll up to category



At SKU level
20OZ MTN DEW → 44OZ REIGN
Support near zero. Thousands of rules, none actionable.



At category level
Packaged Beverages → Salty Snacks
Enough support to act on. A planogram decision.


The GTIN table gives you CATEGORY, SUBCATEGORY, BRAND, and PRODUCT_TYPE. Start at category, go finer only where a rule earns it.

title: Baskets of Goods
text:
FP-Growth finds the rules
Spark’s FPGrowth does the counting. You give it baskets and two thresholds:


Minimum support
How rare an itemset can be before it’s ignored.
We used 0.5%, not the textbook 1%, because baskets are tiny.


Minimum confidence
How weak a rule can be before it’s dropped.
We used 5%, then sorted by lift.


It builds a tree of frequent items instead of rescanning for every combination, so it scales where the textbook Apriori algorithm stalls.

title: Baskets of Goods
section: One more decision before you mine
text:
One more decision before you mine
We ran it on multi-item baskets only: 211,282 of 886,936.

Keep the single-item baskets and support collapses toward zero.
Drop them and every number becomes “out of baskets that had 2 or more items.”


Neither is wrong, but the denominator changes every result. Say which one you used, every time you report a lift.

Example conclusions — one run on the Idaho sample, not a finished analysis.

Segment to sharpen
silver = silver.withColumn("daypart",
    F.when(F.hour("DATE_TIME") < 10, "morning")
     .when(F.hour("DATE_TIME") < 15, "midday")
     .when(F.hour("DATE_TIME") < 20, "evening")
     .otherwise("late"))

morning = baskets_for(silver.filter(F.col("daypart") == "morning"))
Run the same mining per daypart, store, or chain. A rule that only holds at 7am is still a rule — and a better one, because it tells you when to act.

title: Baskets of Goods
text:
Takeaways

Profile first. 56% single-item baskets changes everything downstream.
Roll up to category. SKU-level rules don’t survive contact with a store manager.
Lift, not confidence. Common items fake high confidence.
Write down your cleaning decisions. They move the answer more than the algorithm does.
Rules describe, models predict. The labeled version is its own deck.

What would the store change? What would you measure to know it worked? What cleaning decision could have manufactured your rule?

        "Salty Snacks", "Other Tobacco/Nicotine Products", "Beer"]

    F.first("prior_share"), F.first("days_since"), F.first("bought_before"))

for cat in TOP6:
    train_relevance = train_relevance.withColumn(
        f"y_{slug(cat)}", F.array_contains("cats", cat).cast("int"))
Why six labels and not a softmax. A basket holds several categories at once — the six shares sum to 119%, not 100%. A multiclass model would force them to compete and hand back numbers that cannot be priced.
Why every visit and not just converters. An earlier version trained these on the 13% who came inside and multiplied an attach model in front. Measured against training directly on all visits, the two matched to three decimals, so the extra stage went.

from pyspark.ml.classification import GBTClassifier

models = {}
for cat in TOP6:
    models[cat] = GBTClassifier(featuresCol="features", labelCol=f"y_{slug(cat)}",
                                maxIter=200, maxDepth=6).fit(train_relevance)
Do not rebalance. Base rates run 1.3% to 7.4%; the output is multiplied by dollars, so a model trained 50/50 inflates every expected value. Use weightCol if you must, never SMOTE.
Calibrate. Spark has no built-in calibrator, so fit isotonic regression on a holdout slice. Judge on a reliability curve, not accuracy — calibration is the whole job. Watch for saturation: isotonic is a step function and its top and bottom steps sit at exactly 1 and 0, so clamp both.

Type

the two categories

…among equally frequent non-anchor shoppers

the ratio. Gates

# The comparison group is the whole trick. Every cohort is defined by
# "at least N baskets", so every cohort is a cohort of heavy shoppers
# and indexes high on everything. Hold visit count constant on both sides.
eligible = baskets.groupBy("shopper_id").count().filter("count >= 5")
members  = eligible.join(anchor_regulars, "shopper_id")          # buys A
others   = eligible.join(anchor_regulars, "shopper_id", "left_anti")
796 pairs over 32 anchors. Gate on cohort_index, rank on cohort_rate − other_rate — the ratio alone picks tiny categories, the volume alone picks Candy, which at an index of 1.07 is popular rather than complementary.




customer_scores
Grain: one row per customer-moment in the held-out period. The batch twin of decision — same scoring.py, so the two cannot drift.
fuel_tx | shopper_id | store_id | ts | daypart | fuel_grade | prior_attach
prob_entering | offer_category | personalised | <category>_propensity × 6
top_skus              list[struct{rank, gtin, brand, category,
                                  affinity, p_sku, p_category, p_buys}]
second_category | second_category_skus
                      list[struct{…, cohort_index, excess, headroom}]
583,583 rows, 19 columns. fuel_tx is the primary key: (shopper_id, ts) is not unique — a shopper can have two fuel transactions on one timestamp — and joining on the pair silently fans rows out.
prob_entering is derived, not modelled: 1 − Π(1 − pᵢ) over the six categories, AUC 0.822 against a dedicated attach model’s 0.827. Report it; do not multiply it back into the expected value or the category term counts twice.
No dollar figures in top_skus. The catalog’s margins are average price × an assumed 40%, so they stay in the negotiation code that says so out loud. The ranking is p_buys, which makes the order explainable from the columns beside it.




decision
Grain: one row per candidate offer per fill. The arithmetic that picks one.
Two stages, and the order matters. Stage one picks the category on P(category) alone — the most likely one we are allowed to show. Stage two picks the SKU inside it on expected value. Candidates from any other category never enter this table.
Ranking the whole catalog in one pass looks simpler and is wrong: p_sku is normalised within its category, so a four-SKU category concentrates its probability where a three-hundred-SKU category spreads it thin, and a 2% category with a short tail beats a 90% category with a long one. Those expected values have different denominators and are not comparable.
# Stage one: the category, by relevance. No margin in this step.
allowed = candidates.filter(F.col("in_stock") & F.col("offerable"))
chosen  = (allowed.groupBy("fuel_tx", "category")
    .agg(F.first("p_category").alias("p_category"),
         F.sum("units").alias("cat_units"))        # units break ties
    .withColumn("r", F.row_number().over(
        Window.partitionBy("fuel_tx")
              .orderBy(F.desc("p_category"), F.desc("cat_units"))))
    .filter(F.col("r") == 1).select("fuel_tx", "category"))

# Stage two: the SKU, by economics -- inside that one category.
candidates = allowed.join(chosen, ["fuel_tx", "category"])
EPS = 0.01        # don't bother for less than a cent of expected margin

dec = (candidates
    # Two terms, not three. P(category) is already unconditional --
    # walking inside is inside it -- so an extra p_inside factor
    # would count the same thing twice.
    .withColumn("p_buy", F.col("p_category") * F.col("p_sku"))
    .withColumn("ev_offer", F.col("p_buy_with_offer") *
                            (F.col("unit_margin") - F.col("our_cost")))
    .withColumn("ev_none",  F.col("p_buy") * F.col("unit_margin"))
    .withColumn("uplift_value", F.col("ev_offer") - F.col("ev_none")))

best = (dec.filter(F.col("uplift_value") > EPS)
           .orderBy(F.desc("uplift_value")).limit(1))      # may return nothing
The naive form is wrong. P(buy) × margin − cost never compares against the world where no offer was shown, and it never goes negative while margin beats the discount. The real test is p₁(margin − discount) > p₀ × margin.
p_buy_with_offer is the honest gap: we do not have it. Without a holdout there is no p₁, only p₀, so today this rule runs on an assumed lift and should be labelled as such.
Returning nothing is a valid answer and costs nothing to execute.


The second item
Everything above finds what they buy anyway — the one offer certain to cost margin and change nothing. The pair offer is a third stage against a different table: pair_affinity, built from basket co-occurrence rather than from either model.
# Stage three: the complement. Gate on the ratio, rank on the difference.
pair = (chosen.join(pair_affinity, chosen.category == F.col("anchor"))
    .filter((F.col("cohort_support") >= 200)
            & (F.col("cohort_index") >= 1.05)          # a complement,
            & ~F.col("pair").isin(NOT_OFFERABLE + NOT_PAIRABLE))
    .withColumn("excess", F.col("cohort_rate") - F.col("other_rate"))
    # headroom: don't discount what this shopper already buys every visit
    .join(own_share, ["shopper_id", "pair"], "left")
    .withColumn("headroom", F.lit(1.0) - F.coalesce("own_rate", F.lit(0.0)))
    .withColumn("r", F.row_number().over(
        Window.partitionBy("fuel_tx")
              .orderBy(F.desc(F.col("excess") * F.col("headroom")))))
    .filter(F.col("r") == 1))
cohort_index gates and excess ranks, and both are needed. Volume alone picks the popular item; the ratio alone picks the tiny one. Alcohol is excluded on both sides, so a beer anchor yields no second item — an empty result here is the answer, not a miss.




validation
Grain: not a table you serve — a report you must be able to regenerate. Two models, two different questions, two different checks.
Stage one is judged on calibration, because its output is multiplied by dollars. A model that ranks well but is scaled wrong prices every offer wrong, and AUC would never reveal it.



Decile of predicted P(beverage)
Predicted
Actual

0.0001
0.0005


5

0.0395


9
0.1400
0.1407

Stage two is judged on whether it named the item they bought — hit@10 of 34.3% against the best seller’s 16.9%, both scored on the same rows. Comparing ALS rows against fallback rows would compare two different populations.
# The control that says the harness works: on fallback rows the two
# rankings are the same ranking by construction, so they must agree.
assert (hit[~personalised] == popularity_hit[~personalised]).all()
validate.py runs 116 of these and exits non-zero on any failure; validate_sku.py prints the hit@k breakdown by category.




decision_log
Grain: one row per fill where we could have shown something. This is the table that makes tomorrow’s model possible.



Column
Why
Recoverable later?




fuel_tx, shopper_id, ts
Join key back to the visit
Yes


candidates
What we considered
No


shown_gtin
What we showed, null if nothing
No


propensity
The probability we showed it with
No


is_holdout
Whether this fill was held back
No


model_version
Which models produced it
No



(dec.select("fuel_tx", "shopper_id", "ts", "candidates",
            "shown_gtin", "propensity", "is_holdout", "model_version")
    .write.mode("append").partitionBy("dt").saveAsTable("gold.decision_log"))
Log the propensity or lose the ability to evaluate. Off-policy methods — inverse propensity weighting, doubly robust estimation — all need the probability with which each action was taken. If it was never written down, the information does not exist and no amount of later cleverness recovers it.
This log joins back to visit to produce the next training set, which closes the loop: the system’s own decisions become the data it learns from. That is also why the holdout matters — without it, the model only ever sees the consequences of what it already believed.

title: One Prediction on the Pump Screen
text:
The ask
Ninety seconds. One screen. One offer.

The customer is watching the gallons tick. What do we put in front of them, and how did we decide?

title: One Prediction on the Pump Screen
text:
What the screen knows
The card is read before the fuel flows, so at the moment of the offer we have:


Context
Store, pump, fuel grade, dollars pumped so far, and the hour — in store wall-clock time.


Identity
A shopper id from the card. Every transaction in our extract has one.


History
Whatever that shopper did on previous visits — if there were any.



Anything we can’t know before the nozzle goes back is not a feature. That is the leakage rule with a clock on it.

text:
Where we are going

1 The label. Anchor on fuel, sweep −15/+45, drop the card fees. There is no column for “did they come inside?” — we have to build one.
2 What the data says. Where the signal is, and where it is not. This decides what the models are even allowed to be.
3 Two models. Which category on probability, then which item inside it — plus the checks that say both are working.
4 The economics. Who funds the discount, and when the answer is to show nothing.
5 The second item, which is the one actually worth discounting.


Step 1 is the one everything else inherits. Get the label wrong and every number after it is confident and false.

The label does not exist. We build it.
We want to predict “will this person come inside and buy something?” No column says that. The pump and the counter are two separate transactions — fuel at 10:41, coffee at 10:46 — tied together only by the shopper id and the clock.
So we anchor a window on the fuel transaction and sweep up everything that shopper bought nearby:

Asymmetric on purpose: most people fuel first, and 45 minutes after leaves room for a queue. This is a unit-of-analysis decision, and it is ours to defend — every number in this deck inherits it.

title: One Prediction on the Pump Screen

A trap in the label
First run said 19.4% of fuel visits bought something inside. The top category was SERVICES, at 40% of all conversions.

What SERVICES actually is
99.5% card-processing fees. debitfee, Debit Fee, Card Fee — $0.35, charged on the fuel sale itself.

The fuel transaction was leaking into its own label. A model trained on that learns “customers who pay by card buy SERVICES” — perfectly accurate, perfectly useless.

Look at what our positive class is made of before we train on it. Removing the fees moved the answer by seven points.

Category Relevance · What will they buy?
Six binary classifiers — one per category, fitted over every fuel visit, not only the ones that converted.

A basket holds several categories at once; our six shares sum to 119%, not 100%. A softmax would force them to compete and return numbers we can’t price.



Each model answers one question
P(buys beer on this fill), P(buys a drink on this fill), … — independently, so each is a real probability for its offer. Walking inside is already inside that number.

Where the person enters
Per category, from visits before this one: bought it before? what share of prior baskets? how long since?

GBTClassifier here — this is where interactions live. Beer on a Friday evening.

Candy is 18.2% of every second item in a drink basket, which makes it look like the obvious pair. Drink regulars buy it 1.07× as often as shoppers who come in just as much and don’t buy drinks. It is not a complement — it is just everywhere.

Compared against shoppers who come in just as often but don’t buy the anchor — without that control every cohort indexes high on everything, because every cohort is a cohort of heavy shoppers.

And this is the one claim we cannot settle
Scored on held-out data, our pair offer lands 10.8% against 14.0% for simply picking the most popular second category. That is by design — where a shopper already buys salty snacks constantly we steer elsewhere — but it means we trade a 26% chance of naming something they’d have bought anyway for a 4.5% chance on something incremental. title: One Prediction on the Pump Screen
text:
What we cannot claim
Every number above is a prediction, not a causal effect. We have shown what people do, not what an offer would change.


The gap
A high score says this person buys drinks. It does not say a discount makes them buy one. Nothing in our data separates the two.


What exists
The discounts table has real promotions — loyalty, mix & match, retailer promo — with observable outcomes.


Why it isn’t enough
Assignment wasn’t random. Stores promoted what they expected to sell, so the comparison is biased.


The one thing we need from you: a holdout. Some pumps show no offer. Without it, uplift is not measurable — by us or by anyone.

title: One Prediction on the Pump Screen
section: Could we measure it from what we have?
text:
Could we measure it from what we have?
The discounts table records redemptions, not impressions — 9.2M discounts applied, and zero records of an offer shown and declined. P(buy | offered) has no denominator.
Stores switched promotions on at different dates, though, and that stagger is a natural experiment. Monster’s share of beverage lines gives a clean +1.7 points for treated stores.

We should not believe it
Store count goes 49 → 280 at week zero: almost nobody has a pre-period. The rising pre-trend is different stores entering the average, not behaviour changing — and the share was climbing before the promo and plateaus after, the opposite of the shape a causal effect makes.


The design is sound. This estimate is not. A balanced panel of late adopters would fix it — and that is a better argument for the holdout than any amount of methodology.

title: One Prediction on the Pump Screen
text:
The build order

1 The visit table. Anchor on fuel, sweep −15/+45, drop the card fees. Everything below depends on this being right.
2 Category Relevance. Six calibrated models. The best-seller fallback ships with it, because it carries ~68% of fills.
3 SKU Affinity where the tail justifies it.
4 The expected value rule, priced against showing nothing — and the funding share that decides who pays.
5 The second item. The complement table, which is where a discount can actually change a basket.
6 The holdout, then uplift in dollars.


Steps 1 to 3 are the engineering. Steps 4 to 6 are where the money is — and step 6 is the one we cannot do without you.

What makes data “big”?



Volume
Size on disk. If it fits and runs on your laptop, it isn’t big. Today, hundreds of GB signals big.



Variety
Many types of data: photos, video, spatial, time series, text. Each needs its own storage and retrieval.



Velocity
How fast data arrives: sensors at thousands of readings a second, card transactions.


Usually two of the three earn the word “big.”

This course focuses on simplified volume and velocity: batch processing toward a predictive model, not streaming or real-time decisions.

What Parquet gives you

Columnar: read only the columns you need.
Compressed: similar values sit together, so they compress well.
Typed schema: numbers stay numbers. Nested lists and structs stay nested.
Statistics: min and max per chunk let tools skip data a filter can’t match.
Open standard: Polars, pandas, DuckDB, Spark, R, and Databricks all read it.

title: Data Sizes, Formats, and Tools
section: Parquet on disk, Arrow in memory
text:
Parquet on disk, Arrow in memory



Apache Parquet
A file format. Compressed and encoded for storage. Built to be small and fast to scan.



Apache Arrow
A memory format. Columnar and uncompressed. Built for fast computation.



disk: .parquet → memory: Arrow columns → Polars · pandas · DuckDB · Spark

title: Data Sizes, Formats, and Tools
text:
Why Arrow matters

One shared layout. Tools that speak Arrow can hand data to each other without copying or converting it.
Polars is built on Arrow. Its DataFrames are Arrow columns.
Spark uses Arrow to move data to and from pandas (toPandas(), pandas UDFs).
Columnar in memory means fast operations on whole columns at once.


Parquet is how data rests. Arrow is how data moves and gets computed.

title: Data Sizes, Formats, and Tools
text:
The same question in both
Total visits to religious buildings by state:

PolarsPySpark


import polars as pl

places = pl.scan_parquet("places.parquet")
patterns = pl.scan_parquet("patterns.parquet")

(places
    .filter(pl.col("top_category") == "Religious Organizations")
    .join(patterns, on="placekey")
    .group_by("region")
    .agg(pl.col("raw_visit_counts").sum().alias("visits"))
    .collect())


from pyspark.sql import functions as F

places = spark.read.parquet("places.parquet")
patterns = spark.read.parquet("patterns.parquet")

(places
    .filter(F.col("top_category") == "Religious Organizations")
    .join(patterns, on="placekey")
    .groupBy("region")
    .agg(F.sum("raw_visit_counts").alias("visits"))
    .show())



Both return GA: 4,476,806 and UT: 1,157,708 on the challenge data.

title: Data Sizes, Formats, and Tools
text:
Both are lazy
Nothing runs until you ask for a result (.collect() in Polars, .show() in Spark). First, the tool plans the query:
Parquet SCAN [places.parquet]
  PROJECT 3/25 COLUMNS
  SELECTION: col("top_category") == "Religious Organizations"
Parquet SCAN [patterns.parquet]
  PROJECT 2/22 COLUMNS
The planner read 5 of 47 columns and filtered while scanning. That’s Parquet and a lazy engine working together.

Why this is the feature-engineering skill

Your unit of analysis decides which one you need.
groupBy builds the table: one row per shopper, store, or week.
over(Window) adds context without collapsing: this basket vs. that shopper’s average.
partitionBy + orderBy gives you lags, ranks and running totals — the temporal features.


If you can’t say whether a calculation changes the row count, you don’t know what you’re building yet.

transaction-items-all
128,599,042 rows, one per item rung up, across 71.7M transactions and 940 stores.
pl.scan_parquet("transaction-items-all/*.parquet").select(
    "TRANSACTION_SET_ID",  # the basket key
    "STORE_ID", "DATE_TIME",
    "GTIN",                # barcode, or a placeholder when keyed
    "UNIT_QUANTITY", "GRAND_TOTAL_AMOUNT",
    "SCAN_TYPE",           # GTIN | NONSCAN | PLU | FMT_ERR
    "NONSCAN_CATEGORY",    # NACS dept for keyed lines — FUEL lives here
    "NONSCAN_SUBCATEGORY", # fuel grade lives here
)
58.9% of lines are scanned barcodes; the rest are keyed departments. Fuel is 28% of lines and $1.55B of $2.08B revenue.




shopper-id
71,790,254 rows, one per payment. Every transaction in this extract has a shopper — the unidentified ones were dropped before delivery.
shopper = (pl.scan_parquet("shopper-id/*.parquet")
    .select("TRANSACTION_SET_ID", "SHOPPER_ID")
    .unique(subset="TRANSACTION_SET_ID"))  # split tender → duplicate rows
SHOPPER_ID is hash(card BIN + last 4 + store state). Two consequences worth stating to a client:

The same card in two states is two shoppers, so cross-border travel is invisible.
BIN + last 4 is not unique to a card, so a few ids are more than one person.

8.0M shoppers, median 2 transactions each.




master-gtin
99,074 products, one row per barcode, 35 PDI categories.
gtin = (pl.scan_parquet("master-gtin/*.parquet")
    .select("GTIN", "CATEGORY", "SUBCATEGORY", "BRAND")
    .unique(subset="GTIN"))
Matches 88% of scanned lines. Two cautions:

CATEGORY is PDI’s taxonomy; NONSCAN_CATEGORY is NACS. Coalescing them mixes vocabularies.
Every row was last updated 2024-07-03, before our transaction window opens. Products launched since will never match.

Clean lines
Two filters and a coalesce. This is the whole of it:
lines = (items
    .filter((pl.col("UNIT_QUANTITY").cast(pl.Float64) > 0)
            & (pl.col("GRAND_TOTAL_AMOUNT").cast(pl.Float64) > 0))
    .join(gtin, on="GTIN", how="left")
    .with_columns(category=pl.coalesce("CATEGORY", "NONSCAN_CATEGORY"))
    .drop_nulls("category"))
The filters remove 481,568 voids and 701,406 returns. The coalesce labels 85.6% of lines; the rest are scanned items missing from the master.
Every money column is Decimal(38, x). Cast to Float64 on read or the arithmetic is slow and occasionally surprising.




Drop non-purchases
The rule is not “drop SERVICES”. It is drop anything the customer didn’t choose.
NOT_A_PURCHASE = ["FUEL", "SERVICES"]   # fuel is the anchor, not the outcome

Fuel visit
The unit of analysis, and the decision a team has to defend. A visit is every purchase by the same shopper from 15 minutes before the fuel transaction to 45 minutes after.
BEFORE, AFTER = 15, 45

# Hour buckets keep the join small; the window spans at most three of them,
# so each candidate is offered to its bucket and both neighbours.
shifted = pl.concat([
    store.with_columns(bucket=pl.col("bucket") + pl.duration(hours=k))
    for k in (-1, 0, 1)])

delta = (pl.col("ts_store") - pl.col("ts")).dt.total_minutes()
hit = fuel.join(shifted, on=["SHOPPER_ID", "bucket"], how="left").filter(
    (delta >= -BEFORE) & (delta <= AFTER))

36,142,617 fuel visits. 12.8% buy something inside. Median in-store spend when they do: $7.87.
basket = fuel.join(
    hit.group_by("fuel_tx").agg(n_store_tx=pl.col("store_tx").n_unique()),

This column does not exist in the data. We built it, and every number downstream inherits whatever we got wrong here. That is why the window and the SERVICES filter are worth a slide each.
About 1 in 8 — the base rate every model has to beat.

Everything knowable before the nozzle goes back. The card is read before the fuel flows, so identity is available too.

    hour=pl.col("ts").dt.hour(),        # store wall-clock, per PDI
    weekday=pl.col("ts").dt.weekday(),

)

History features
Per category, computed strictly from visits before the one being scored. This is the leakage rule with a clock on it.
from pyspark.sql import Window
w = (Window.partitionBy("SHOPPER_ID", "category")
          .orderBy("ts").rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, -1))

df = (df
  .withColumn("bought_before", F.max("bought").over(w))
  .withColumn("prior_share",   F.avg("bought").over(w))
  .withColumn("days_since",    F.datediff("ts", F.max("ts").over(w))))
rowsBetween(..., -1) is the whole trick — it excludes the current row.
History barely predicts whether they come inside (12.6% with none, 12.5% with 10+), but it is the best signal for what they buy. That asymmetry is why there are two models instead of one.




Category Relevance
Will they buy category X on this fill? Classification — six calibrated binary classifiers (HistGradientBoostingClassifier), one per category, each scoring every visit.
for cat in TOP6:                       # six independent binaries
    y = F.array_contains("cats", cat).cast("int")
    models[cat] = GBTClassifier(labelCol="y").fit(train.withColumn("y", y))
Not a multiclass model. A basket holds several categories at once, so a softmax would force them to compete and return numbers we cannot price.
Not rebalanced. The output is multiplied by dollars; a model trained on a balanced sample scores an average visit at 0.5 instead of its base rate and inflates every expected value about 4×.
The strongest single feature is the shopper’s own prior attach rate. How many times we have seen someone is worth +0.004 AUC; what share of those visits ended inside is worth +0.109.

Which item inside the category? Alternating least squares on implicit feedback — Hu, Koren & Volinsky (2008).
als = ALS(userCol="shopper_ix", itemCol="item_ix", ratingCol="n",
          implicitPrefs=True,        # counts are confidence, not ratings
          rank=32, regParam=0.05, alpha=20, coldStartStrategy="drop")
The item key is gtin@daypart. ALS takes no features, so the only way to give it a clock is to put one in the key — and the clock matters: same-daypart purchase pairs repeat the same SKU 18.0% of the time against 10.0% across dayparts.
SKU, not brand. At brand level ALS scores 0.88× popularity — worse than showing the best seller. With a handful of brands that matter there is nothing personal left to learn; the long tail of SKUs is what gives the model something to do.

Scores are normalised within a category, so the number means given they buy this category, which item — which is what the decision multiplies against P(category).
This model only ever ranks inside one category. Category Relevance picks the category first, on probability alone, and SKU Affinity is confined to it. Ranking the whole catalog by expected value instead lets a narrow, high-margin category beat a wide, high-probability one on a technicality — its p_sku denominator is smaller — and offers candy to a customer we are 90.6% sure wants a beverage.




Best-Seller
The popularity ranking — and the path for about 68% of fills.
You enter the ALS factor matrix only by having bought in that category before the cutoff. Most fuel customers never did:

raw = popularity[daypart_items]        # no factors for this shopper
This is not a degraded path, it is the primary one. Build it first: the personalised tier is an improvement on top of a fallback you need anyway, and the vendor-funded revenue does not depend on ALS — it depends on going to SKU granularity at all.




Stage one · the category
Relevance decides this, on probability alone. Six calibrated models give six unconditional probabilities; we take the highest one we are allowed to show.
allowed = [c for c in categories
           if c not in NOT_OFFERABLE          # tobacco: a business rule
           and in_stock_and_offerable(c)]     # something to actually sell
category = max(allowed, key=lambda c: p_category[c])
Margin does not get a vote here. Let expected value pick the category and a narrow, high-margin category beats a wide, high-probability one on nothing but a shorter SKU tail — p_sku is normalised within a category, so a four-SKU category concentrates its probability where a three-hundred-SKU one spreads it thin. That is how a customer we are 90% sure wants a beverage ends up being offered candy.
Ties go to the daypart’s best seller, not to the alphabet. Before that rule a shopper with every category at the probability floor — someone who has fuelled a thousand times and never walked in — was shown beer, because “Beer” sorts first.




Stage two · the SKU
Rank the SKUs inside that one category. A SKU from any other category cannot appear, however profitable.
p_sku  = raw / raw.sum()          # normalised within the category
p_buys = p_category * p_sku       # P(buys this exact SKU on this fill)
order  = argsort(-p_buys)[:10]
Ranked on probability, not on expected value. The catalog’s margins are average price × an assumed 40% — the PDI extract has no cost column — so ranking on EV would let an assumption choose the item. The margin terms ride along for the funding conversation; they do not set the order.
in_stock and offerable filter the candidates; they do not change the denominator. P(sku | category) is a conditional over every SKU in the category, and excluding tobacco by business rule should not inflate what is left.
The same function serves the live fill and the batch table — scoring.py. Two copies of this ranking drifted twice, and both times the written table disagreed with the live answer.




Pair affinity
A different table answering a different question: not what will they buy, but what SECOND thing could a discount add to the basket.

What it is for

Controlling exposure is the whole trick. Every cohort is defined as “at least five purchase baskets”, so every cohort is a cohort of heavy shoppers and indexes high on nearly everything. The first cut had drink regulars over-indexing on frozen food at 6.1× — pure visit frequency. Comparing against shoppers who buy just as often and do not buy the anchor divides that out.
Gate on the index, rank on the excess. Volume alone picks the popular item: Candy is 18.2% of every second item in a drink basket and looks obvious, but its index is 1.07 — not a complement, just everywhere. The index alone picks the tiny one.

The naive form is wrong:
P(buys) × margin − cost        ← never negative while margin > discount
It never asks what would have happened with no offer. The real comparison is between two worlds:

Margin and lift are assumptions; the data has no cost column. The $3.25 and $0.90 are real.




The pump screen
One offer, or none. The constraints the product has to live inside:

Fire during the fill. 77% of in-store purchases happen within five minutes of the fuel transaction.
16.2% already shopped before fuelling. They are not addressable by a pump screen, so your real audience is the other 84%.
Ninety seconds, one screen, and a customer watching the gallons tick.

Showing nothing is a legitimate output. It needs no model to execute and it never loses money — which makes it the baseline every offer must beat.




Holdout
This does not exist, and it is the single thing worth asking Murphy for.
A slice of pumps that show no offer, assigned at random. Without it you can measure what people do, never what an offer changed.
# Random at the visit level, logged with the decision.
holdout = F.hash("fuel_tx") % 100 < 5     # 5% see nothing
Log the offer you showed and the probability you showed it with. Without logged propensities you cannot evaluate offline later, and that mistake is unrecoverable — the information was never captured.
With a holdout you can finally model uplift rather than propensity, and separate the persuadable customers from the ones who would have bought anyway.

3 · The check that carries weight
Sections 1 and 2 are illustrations. This is the section that decides whether any of it can be used, and it is worth saying why.
An offer is chosen by multiplying a probability by dollars. That makes ranking accuracy almost irrelevant and scale accuracy everything: a model that sorts customers perfectly but reports 0.34 where the truth is 0.20 will rank the right person first and then price the offer 70% too high. AUC cannot see that error at all — it is invariant to any monotone rescaling of the scores. Calibration is the only check that looks at it.

The middle of the distribution is calibrated to within a tenth of a point. The top decile is the one to watch: at a predicted 34.3% the observed rate is 32.9%, so the model is mildly over-confident exactly where it is most willing to spend money. That is the right direction to be wrong in for a sceptic and the wrong direction for a budget — an offer priced off the top decile is buying about 4% less attach than the arithmetic assumes.
The bottom three deciles run slightly under-confident, which is the signature of isotonic calibration flattening at the floor.

What we can conclude from this
The probabilities can be used as probabilities. Through the middle of the distribution predicted and observed agree to within a tenth of a point, so multiplying them by a margin is legitimate arithmetic rather than a rescaling of a score. That is the permission this whole pipeline needs.
Discount any budget built off the top decile by about 4%. Predicted 34.3% against an observed 32.9% is a 1.4-point gap — small absolutely, but it sits precisely where we are most willing to spend, so it is the error that costs money. It is also the safe direction to be wrong in: we overestimate the value of the offers we are keenest on, rather than missing good ones.
The under-confidence at the bottom is harmless. Those are customers we would not offer to anyway; being slightly pessimistic about someone we were going to show nothing to changes no decision.


What it does not let us conclude
Calibration says our prediction of what they do anyway is accurate. It says nothing about what an offer changes — p₁ appears nowhere in it. A perfectly calibrated model of the status quo is still no evidence that a discount moves anybody, which is why the holdout remains the ask.


And stage two: did it name the item they bought?

7 · SKU Affinity (ALS)

Stage one has already settled the category
The six probabilities above pick it: the most likely category we are allowed to show. For this shopper that is Packaged Beverages at 0.6782. Stage two may only look inside it.
That restriction is deliberate. An earlier version ranked the whole catalog in one pass by expected value, and offered candy to a customer the model was 90.6% sure wanted a beverage. Not a coding bug — a denominator. p_sku is normalised within its category, so a four-SKU category concentrates its probability into four numbers while beverages spread theirs across hundreds. A 2% category with a short tail out-earns a 90% category with a long one, and the two expected values were never comparable in the first place.
So: relevance picks the category, economics picks the item inside it. Margin cannot overrule relevance. Ties in stage one — a brand-new customer is at the probability floor in all six — go to the daypart’s best-selling category, because otherwise the alphabet decides and “Beer” wins.

Two gaps this page cannot close
No logged propensity. A production version must write down what it showed and the probability it showed it with. Without that, off-policy evaluation is impossible later and the information cannot be reconstructed after the fact — it is the cheapest thing on this list and the easiest to forget.
Assumed margins. unit_margin is average price × 40%. The extract has no cost column, so every dollar figure here moves the moment someone supplies real ones. The probabilities do not.

text:
Where we are
Rules found what sells together. Labels predicted one outcome.

Segmentation asks a different question: who are these customers, and how many kinds are there?

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
Unlabeled learning
There is no Y. No right answer to train against, so nothing to score yourself against at the end.


Supervised
You know the answer for past rows. The model learns to reproduce it.
Did this visit include fuel?


Unsupervised
You have only the features. The model looks for structure.
What kinds of shoppers are there?


That freedom is the danger: an algorithm will always return groups, whether or not they mean anything.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
Clustering

Partitioning a set of objects into groups so that objects in the same group are more similar to each other than to those in other groups.

The analyst defines “similar.” That choice — which features, on what scale — decides the answer more than the algorithm does.

Clusters are a hypothesis, not a finding. You still have to show they’re stable and that someone can act on them.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
k-means vs. HDBSCAN

Illustrative: make_moons and make_blobs from scikit-learn, not customer data.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
What the picture shows



k-means

You must pick k in advance
Cuts by distance to a centre, so it only finds round blobs
Every point gets a cluster, outliers included




HDBSCAN

Finds the number of clusters itself
Follows density, so shapes can be anything
Points in sparse regions are labeled noise, not forced



For customers, “I don’t know how many segments there are” and “some shoppers fit no segment” are both honest, so HDBSCAN fits the problem.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
The two knobs

min_cluster_size — the smallest group you’ll accept as a segment. Larger values are more robust on noisy data.
min_samples — how dense a neighborhood must be for a point to count as core. Higher means more points called noise. Defaults to min_cluster_size; tune it second.

labels = HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=100, min_samples=20).fit_predict(X)
For a customer product, set min_cluster_size to your privacy floor: no segment smaller than the number of shoppers you’re willing to report on.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
The curse of dimensionality
With 20 behavioral features per shopper, distance stops meaning much: in high dimensions, everything is far from everything, and “nearest neighbor” loses its edge over the average point.

Distances concentrate, so density looks flat
Sparse space, so clusters have no room to be dense
Compute cost grows with every column

Dimension reduction maps the data to fewer dimensions while keeping what matters: which points are near which.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
UMAP
Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection.

Find each point’s nearest neighbors in the original high-dimensional space.
Build a graph of those neighbor relationships.
Lay the graph out in 2 to 5 dimensions, nudging points until the layout preserves the neighborhoods.



n_neighbors
Small keeps local detail. Large keeps the global shape.


min_dist
How tightly points may pack. Low for clustering, higher for a readable picture.


n_components
Output dimensions. 5 to cluster, 2 to draw.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
UMAP on handwritten digits

64 pixel columns, projected to 2. HDBSCAN found 12 clusters with 1.8% noise — close to the 10 true digits, splitting a couple of them.
Illustrative: scikit-learn digits, not customer data.

title: Customer Segmentation
section: Why digits are the honest test
text:
Why digits are the honest test
We know the answer here: 10 digits. So we can see the failure modes you won’t see on customers:

Some digits split into two clusters (different handwriting styles)
Some sit next to each other (4, 7 and 9 overlap)
A few points land in no cluster


On customer data nobody hands you the digits. That’s why stability checks replace accuracy.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
The pipeline


1 Features
~20 per shopper

→

2 Scale
log, standardize

→

3 UMAP → 5-D

→

4 HDBSCAN

→

5 Name them
profile each group


Scaling matters more than it looks. Dollars run to the hundreds and trip counts to single digits, so without scaling, spend decides every cluster.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
Features for a C-Store shopper



Frequency and value: trips, basket total, items per trip
Timing: daypart shares, weekday vs. weekend



Mission: fuel, fountain and food, packaged drinks, snacks, tobacco
Price and payment: discount use, credit vs. debit


Leave store brand out of the features. Otherwise you cluster by where people shop, then “discover” that each brand has its own shoppers.

title: Customer Segmentation
section: Pick the unit of analysis first
text:
Pick the unit of analysis first
One row per what? For segments, it’s one row per shopper, not per basket — but over what span?


One week
A trial run split the segments almost entirely by daypart, because most shoppers made a single trip.


A quarter or more
Enough trips per shopper that frequency, mission and timing can vary within a row.


Example conclusions — from a one-store, one-week sample, not a finished analysis.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
Naming the segments
The model returns 0, 1, 2, -1. You turn those into something a client can use:

Profile each cluster against the features that built it.
Find what makes it different from the average, not what’s biggest in it.
Name it for the behavior: Morning commuters, Fill-up only.
Check the name survives a new quarter of data.


-1 is a real answer. “Unsegmented” shoppers are a group too, and often a big one.

title: Customer Segmentation
section: Spark builds the table, not the clusters
text:
Spark builds the table, not the clusters
UMAP and HDBSCAN are single-machine libraries. Spark ML has k-means, bisecting k-means and Gaussian mixtures — no HDBSCAN.


PySpark
millions of lines → one row per shopper

→

One machine
UMAP + HDBSCAN on the shopper table

→

PySpark
join labels back, profile, write Delta


The heavy lifting is the feature build, and that’s the part Spark is for.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
Why the handoff is fine
The transaction data is big. The shopper table isn’t.


Millions
of transaction lines, across stores and quarters. Spark territory.


~100k rows
one per shopper, with ~20 columns. A few MB in memory.


A table that fits in a driver’s memory doesn’t need a cluster to cluster it. Use Spark to get there, then stop.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
In a Databricks notebook
%pip install umap-learn hdbscan

features = spark.table("workspace.cstore.shopper_features")   # built with Spark
pdf = features.toPandas()                                     # Arrow handles the move

labels = hdbscan.HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=50).fit_predict(
    umap.UMAP(n_components=5, min_dist=0.0).fit_transform(X))

%pip install is notebook-scoped: it installs on the driver for this session.
toPandas() moves everything to the driver. Check the row count first.
Serverless compute gives you a modest driver. If it won’t fit, sample.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
How you know it worked
Without a Y, you check stability and usefulness:

Noise share. If 60% is noise, your features or knobs are wrong.
Across random seeds. Do the same shoppers land together each run?
Across time. Does last quarter’s segment still describe the same people?
Against a simple baseline. Does it beat RFM (recency, frequency, monetary) buckets?
The client test. Can someone name an action per segment? If not, it’s decoration.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
What segmentation can’t do

It won’t tell you why anyone belongs to a group.
It won’t predict what a shopper does next. That’s a labeled model.
It will give you groups even from noise, so a result alone proves nothing.
Segments drift: refit on a schedule and expect the boundaries to move.
